title: Argosy Escalation - Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Follow-up on last week's production incident impacting inference latency and degraded availability for a subset of requests. Reviewed root cause (KV cache eviction + autoscaling race), mitigations shipped (hotfix + scaling policy change), and longer-term reliability improvements and audit items.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Evelyn Carter: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this to ~45 minutes, uh quick checkin on the argosy incident follow up.
[00:00:12] Sara Kim: thanks Evelyn, yeah appreciate it, we had a bunch of customers pinging SRE last thursday, so mostly wanna make sure the fixes are in and timeline for the long term.
[00:00:28] Marcus Li: quick recap — the incident started at 10:43 UTC when our prefix KV cache experienced a coordinated eviction due to a memory pressure event on the pool serving dedicated customers. that triggered a burst of cold-start tokenization and amplification, which hit our autoscaler logic and created a scale-thundering effect.
[00:00:45] Jared Mills: just to interrupt, is that the K V cash eviction you're referring to? the thing in the doc is spelled K V cash in the meeting notes, so wanted to confirm it's KV cache.
[00:00:52] Marcus Li: yes sorry bad transcript there — KV cache, prefix caching.
[00:01:05] Ravi Patel: from security side we got alerts about elevated latencies and some re-tries, nothing looked like data exfil but we want assurance on logs and auditability.
[00:01:18] Priya Anand: timeline wise, hotfix 1 was rolled at 11:05 which changed the eviction threshold and prevented further mass evictions. hotfix 2 at 11:30 changed the autoscaler cooldown and added a temporary manual shard limit. post-rollout latency returned to normal around 11:45.
[00:01:40] Sara Kim: ok good, who owns the permanent fix and what's the plan?
[00:01:48] Marcus Li: root cause is twofold: a mis-tuned LRU for a high-cardinality prefix workload and a subtle regression in the autoscaler heuristics that allowed simultaneous upscales without sufficient stagger. permanent fix is in three parts — 1) a new adaptive cache retention policy that treats large cardinality prefixes differently, 2) autoscaler safety net to limit concurrent scale-up ramps, and 3) better observability (per-prefix cache hit heatmaps).
[00:02:12] Jared Mills: are those changes risky to deploy? we run on Redwood Dedicated so we need an ops window.
[00:02:20] Evelyn Carter: the adaptive policy is low risk — it's config and can be canaried; autoscaler change is medium risk and we'll want a small canary cohort. Marcus, can you outline the rollback plan?
[00:02:34] Marcus Li: rollback is straightforward — revert the config flags and scale the pool down via the admin console; we also have a fallback policy to route to a slightly higher-cost model variant (we referred to that as model-fallback in the call) if the cache warmup takes longer.
[00:02:51] Sara Kim: model fallback is fine as long as we agree on cost alerting.
[00:02:55] Evelyn Carter: noted, we'll add cost guardrails to the runbook.
[00:03:06] Ravi Patel: on the compliance front, can you confirm that audit logs for the incident were preserved and that the KMS keys were not rotated during the window?
[00:03:15] Marcus Li: yes audit logs retained — link to postmortem doc in the notes, and no KMS rotation occurred. I'll circulate a zipped log export for your security team.
[00:03:30] Priya Anand: next steps from our side included updating the incident runbook to include the new cache thresholds, adding a pre-deploy check for high-cardinality prefix patterns, and scheduling a customer-specific benchmark to simulate your workload.
[00:03:47] Sara Kim: that benchmark will be critical. last time our test didn't trigger the same pattern so we need a more realistic workload.
[00:03:56] Marcus Li: agreed, we'll use your anonymized sample traces; Jared, can you share a 1-hour trace of the peak window?
[00:04:05] Jared Mills: yes can do, will scrub PII and upload to the secure share.
[00:04:12] Evelyn Carter: good. quick walk-through of the postmortem doc — link: https://redwood.internal/postmortems/ARG-2027-07-28 — it's summarized in section 2, root cause section 3, mitigation steps section 4.
[00:04:29] Speaker 1: (mumbles) the doc had an odd reference to "Dedicate pool" spelled Dedicate, maybe a transcription thing.
[00:04:34] Marcus Li: yeah some transcripts show Redwood Dedicated as Dedicate, not important.
[00:04:42] Sara Kim: can we get SLA credits or at least a formal acknowledgement?
[00:04:48] Evelyn Carter: we'll review the SLA clause, Priya will own credits discussion and loop in legal if needed.
[00:04:58] Priya Anand: yep, I'll take that.
[00:05:04] Ravi Patel: I'd like a bit more detail on grey failures — what monitoring will detect early signs so we don't hit a full outage.
[00:05:12] Marcus Li: we will add two new alerts: per-prefix cache hit rate dropping below threshold, and per-pool sudden increase in cold-token count. both tie into the runbook and will auto-open a pagerduty incident to oncall.
[00:05:27] Sara Kim: will those alerts cause any automated mitigation?
[00:05:30] Marcus Li: initially they'll be paging only, but we have a second tier that can throttle low-priority requests or route them to a burst pool to reduce pressure. automated routing is disabled by default and would be opt-in; we can enable it for Argosy if you want.
[00:05:44] Jared Mills: prefer manual first, but open to a controlled opt-in after we validate the canary.
[00:05:50] Evelyn Carter: agreed. timeline for the permanent fixes — engineering estimates: adaptive cache policy PR in 2 weeks, autoscaler change in 3 weeks, observability dashboards in 1 week. targeted full deployment to staging in 3 weeks and production rollout, with canary, in 4 weeks.
[00:06:10] Sara Kim: sounds reasonable. can you walk me through the canary plan?
[00:06:14] Marcus Li: canary will be a small percentage of traffic routed to updated config, monitored for 24h with automatic rollback if cache hit rate drops or latency increases beyond SLOs. we'll start with 1% traffic for 12 hours, then 5% for 12 hours, and so on.
[00:06:30] Ravi Patel: what about log retention and forensic artifacts for compliance audits?
[00:06:35] Marcus Li: we'll retain full raw traces for 90 days for your account and provide a forensic export if needed. everything is logged with request IDs and TLS preserved; we use customer-managed KMS for keys when configured.
[00:06:51] Sara Kim: good. any blockers?
[00:06:55] Marcus Li: dependency on a small kernel patch in our runtime that's already PR'd; we want to validate perf on a dedicated instance. it's low-risk but requires a short maintenance window.
[00:07:07] Evelyn Carter: can we schedule the maintenance for next Tuesday 03:00 UTC?
[00:07:12] Jared Mills: that's ok for us.
[00:07:16] Priya Anand: action: schedule maintenance, I'll send calendar invite.
[00:07:22] Evelyn Carter: other items — we noted some confusion around the "model fallback" option and cost implications. Marcus, please provide a cost estimate for fallback for typical Argosy traffic.
[00:07:33] Marcus Li: yes I'll produce a small spreadsheet showing delta cost per 100k tokens and an hourly estimate for the 1%/5% canary scenarios.
[00:07:42] Sara Kim: also, can we get a one-page runbook tailored to our SREs? the postmortem doc is thorough but we want a quick checklist.
[00:07:50] Evelyn Carter: Priya will supply a 1-page playbook.
[00:07:54] Ravi Patel: security asks: can you confirm SSO/SAML assertions and RBAC for who can flip those autoscaler flags? we need admin-level control limited to two people on our side.
[00:08:05] Marcus Li: yes the admin console integrates with SAML; we can add RBAC roles so only designated Argosy admins can change scaling flags. we'll map the role to two user emails.
[00:08:16] Jared Mills: we'll send those emails.
[00:08:20] Evelyn Carter: recapping next steps...
[00:08:24] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) send the runbook and the logs, cost estimate spreadsheet, schedule maintenance, canary plan.
[00:08:33] Evelyn Carter: exactly — we'll push updates by the dates below. any other questions?
[00:08:39] Sara Kim: one more — do we recommend Dedicated or Private for this workload long-term? given we're concerned about predictable performance.
[00:08:47] Marcus Li: Dedicated is still fine with the improvements; Private gives you more isolation but higher ops overhead and cost. we can do a comparative TCO after the canary.
[00:09:00] Priya Anand: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifact links and action items.
[00:09:07] Evelyn Carter: thanks all, meeting adjourned.
